title: Registration and device-enrollment data can link the homeowner to specific home devices
description: The flow carries account-registration details together with camera/sensor enrollment information into the Home Hub. If identifiers such as email, account ID, serial numbers, MAC addresses, or device names are transmitted or bound together, the hub can create a persistent association between the homeowner and a set of in-home devices, increasing linkability across setup, later usage, and support/maintenance contexts.
assumptions: Assumes the enrollment payload includes stable account and device identifiers and that the hub stores or further uses this association.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort based on standard LINDDUN linkability decomposition; exact sub-node naming may vary by version.

title: Enrollment metadata may identify the homeowner or household
description: Account registration commonly includes directly identifying data such as name, email address, phone number, postal address, or payment-related details. Even if direct identifiers are minimized, the set of enrolled devices and their identifiers can uniquely identify a household when combined with other records, allowing the Home Hub or connected ecosystem to identify the data subject.
assumptions: Assumes registration includes direct or indirect identifiers, or that the device inventory is sufficiently unique to act as an identifier.
uncertainty_note: Exact fields are not specified in the flow description, so this is inferred from typical account-registration and smart-home enrollment practices.

title: Setup data may disclose sensitive household information beyond what is necessary
description: During registration and camera/sensor enrollment, the homeowner may disclose device types, count, placement labels, room names, occupancy-related settings, and home topology information. This can reveal intimate details about the household, security posture, routines, or presence of children/elderly residents, exceeding what is necessary for basic onboarding if not minimized.
assumptions: Assumes the enrollment process collects device metadata such as device class, location labels, or configuration details.
uncertainty_note: The specific enrollment fields are not provided; threat applies if onboarding captures rich metadata, which is common in smart-home setup.

title: The homeowner may not be adequately informed about what personal data is collected during onboarding
description: If the Home Hub does not clearly explain during registration and enrollment which personal data is collected, for what purposes, for how long it is retained, and with whom it is shared, the homeowner lacks sufficient awareness to make an informed choice. This is especially relevant because device-enrollment data can implicitly reveal household composition and behavior patterns.
assumptions: Assumes onboarding UX may not provide granular just-in-time notices for registration and device-enrollment fields.
uncertainty_note: This is a plausible threat for the flow, but whether it materializes depends on the actual notice/UX design.

title: Registration and enrollment may be used for secondary purposes without explicit user understanding or control
description: Data provided to create an account and enroll cameras/sensors may later be used for analytics, product improvement, targeted offers, cross-device profiling, or sharing with ecosystem partners. If the flow does not separate mandatory setup data from optional uses, the homeowner may unknowingly consent to broader processing than expected.
assumptions: Assumes the system or associated services may reuse onboarding data beyond strict account provisioning and device setup.
uncertainty_note: Secondary-use risk is common in connected-device ecosystems, but the description does not confirm such downstream use.

title: Account creation and device enrollment may collect more personal data than is necessary or without a valid legal basis
description: If the Home Hub requires excessive personal details or enrolls devices with unnecessary metadata during setup, the collection may violate data-minimization, purpose-limitation, or lawful-basis requirements. Examples include requiring precise home-location details, persistent hardware identifiers, or optional profiling data when basic onboarding could be completed with less information.
assumptions: Assumes the onboarding design may request optional or excessive data and that compliance controls are not already in place.
uncertainty_note: Compliance assessment depends on jurisdiction and actual data fields, so this is a general privacy-compliance threat rather than a confirmed violation.

title: Temporary access code may be intercepted in transit to the Home Hub
description: The guest submits a temporary access code to the Home Hub. If this communication is observable by unauthorized parties (e.g., insecure wireless channel, exposed keypad/bus, or nearby eavesdropping on a companion interface), the code can reveal information associated with the guest's visit and access event. This is an information-disclosure privacy threat on the incoming flow to the process.
assumptions: Assumes the code entry traverses or is exposed over an interface that can be observed beyond the guest and the Home Hub; purely local sealed keypad entry would reduce this risk.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selected by best judgement; retrieved context confirms I applies to ExternalEntity->Process flows but does not provide the exact subtree node for this scenario.

title: Observing submission of a temporary code can reveal a guest's participation
description: The mere existence of this flow—someone entering a temporary access code at the Home Hub—can allow an observer to infer that a guest is currently present, expected, or attempting entry, even without learning the code value. This fits a detectability threat because system interaction existence and timing can expose data-subject involvement.
assumptions: Assumes an attacker can observe the interaction itself, such as seeing keypad use, radio traffic, network packets, or device status changes at the Home Hub.
uncertainty_note: The applicability of detectability is strong from LINDDUN methodology, but the exact tree node is chosen by best judgement because the retrieved context did not include detailed node ids.

title: Temporary access code entry may enable linking repeated visits by the same guest
description: If the Home Hub or surrounding observers can correlate repeated use of the same temporary code, entry pattern, or associated metadata, separate access events may be linked to the same guest or household relationship. This can undermine unlinkability of guest visits across time.
assumptions: Assumes codes are reused, stable for a period, or accompanied by correlatable metadata such as timestamp patterns or device/interface identifiers.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on code reuse or persistent identifiers; if each code is one-time and no correlatable metadata is exposed, the risk may be negligible. Tree node is best-effort.

title: Guest may not be adequately informed how temporary access code data is processed
description: When entering a temporary access code, the guest may not receive sufficient notice about what data the Home Hub collects from the interaction, how long it is retained, whether failed attempts are logged, or who can access these logs. Lack of transparency and consent/choice around this collection is a non-compliance risk.
assumptions: Assumes the system logs or otherwise processes the code-entry event and that guest-facing notice/consent mechanisms are absent or insufficient.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends on applicable legal basis and jurisdiction. Exact node id is selected by best judgement.

title: Local event log retains evidence of occupants' actions
description: Writing motion, door, and other sensor events to a persistent local event log creates retained evidence about actions and events in the home, such as entry/exit, movement, and presence patterns. This can undermine deniability because the datastore preserves records that may later be used to prove that a particular event or behavior occurred.
assumptions: The local event log stores event records persistently for some period and those records can be accessed later by an operator, household member, maintainer, or attacker with access to the hub or storage.

title: Event log enables inference of household behavior and presence
description: A local log of motion, door, and sensor events can disclose sensitive information about residents' private lives, including occupancy, routines, sleep/wake cycles, arrivals/departures, and room usage. Even if the flow only records raw events, the accumulated datastore content reveals intimate behavioral patterns.
assumptions: Event timestamps and sensor identifiers or locations are stored with sufficient granularity to reconstruct behavior over time.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selected by best judgement from LINDDUN disclosure threat structure; exact sub-node may vary depending on the project's threat-tree version.

title: Cross-event correlation can link sensor events to a specific household or person
description: Persistently storing multiple sensor events in one local log allows correlation across time and sensor types. This may link otherwise separate observations into a coherent profile of a particular household, resident, or visitor, increasing the ability to single out or track individuals associated with the home.
assumptions: The log includes stable device, room, household, or user-associated context that lets events be correlated to the same environment or person over time.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on whether logged events can reasonably be tied to identifiable residents rather than remaining purely anonymous device telemetry.

title: Residents may be unaware that detailed sensor events are logged locally
description: If the Home Hub writes detailed motion, door, and other sensor events to a local event log without clear notice, residents and visitors may not realize that their in-home activities are being recorded and retained. This creates a detectability issue because the existence and extent of logging may not be apparent to data subjects.
assumptions: The product does not provide sufficiently visible indicators, notices, or accessible interfaces showing that these events are being logged and retained.
uncertainty_note: Exact detectability node may differ by LINDDUN Pro version; selected node reflects hidden/insufficiently visible processing.

title: Log format or retention may be unintelligible to residents
description: Even if users are told that events are logged, the meaning, granularity, and retention implications of motion/door/sensor event records may be difficult for residents to understand. Technical labels, timestamps, and device identifiers can make the privacy impact of the datastore unclear, undermining users' ability to form an accurate understanding of the processing.
assumptions: Log entries or privacy notices are presented in a technical or incomplete way that ordinary residents cannot readily interpret.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selected by best judgement because no specific usability-tree excerpt was provided in context.

title: Local logging may exceed expectations or lack valid consent/legal basis
description: Recording detailed in-home sensor events in a persistent local datastore may constitute processing beyond what residents or visitors reasonably expect, especially for visitors or secondary household members who did not actively agree to such logging. If consent, transparency, purpose limitation, or another legal basis is not adequately established, the flow can create a non-compliance risk.
assumptions: The deployment involves jurisdictions or policies requiring notice/consent or another valid legal basis for collecting and retaining in-home behavioral event data.
uncertainty_note: This is a privacy-compliance threat based on plausible governance obligations; actual applicability depends on deployment context, roles, and jurisdiction.

title: Upload of identifiable video clips enables identification of residents and visitors
description: Recorded camera clips uploaded from the Home Hub to cloud storage can contain directly or indirectly identifying personal data such as faces, voices, timestamps, and location/context of the home. Centralizing these clips in cloud storage increases the ability to identify data subjects from the uploaded content.
assumptions: Camera clips contain people or other identifying contextual information and are associated with a household account.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node id is based on best judgement from LINDDUN identification threats; retrieved context did not include the specific identification subtree.

title: Cloud upload of clips enables linkage of events and behaviors over time
description: Repeated uploads of recorded clips from the Home Hub to the same cloud video store can be linked to one another by account, device identifiers, timestamps, and metadata. This can allow reconstruction of household routines, visitor patterns, and occupancy behavior across time.
assumptions: Uploads carry stable identifiers, account context, timestamps, or other metadata that permit correlation.
uncertainty_note: Specific linkage node id is selected by best judgement; retrieved context did not provide the linkage subtree.

title: Stored cloud video clips may be accessible more broadly than necessary
description: Once uploaded, personal video clips in cloud storage may be exposed to cloud administrators, internal services, third-party processors, or overly broad account-sharing settings. This would disclose highly sensitive household video data beyond what is necessary for storage and retrieval.
assumptions: Cloud storage or associated access controls may permit access by multiple roles or services beyond the primary user.

title: Insufficient proof of upload consent or user action for cloud storage
description: If the Home Hub uploads clips automatically without reliable records of the user's consent, configuration choice, or explicit triggering action, users may later be unable to prove they did not intend certain recordings to be sent to cloud storage, or the provider may be unable to demonstrate valid authorization for the upload.
assumptions: Upload can occur automatically based on device settings, motion events, or default configuration.
uncertainty_note: Non-repudiation subtree id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include specific Nr nodes.

title: Users may be unaware that recorded clips are uploaded to the cloud
description: The Home Hub may send recorded camera clips to cloud video storage automatically or in the background. If this behavior is not clearly visible at the time of recording or upload, residents and visitors may be unaware that local recordings are being transferred and retained remotely.
assumptions: The system may not provide sufficiently clear notices, indicators, or just-in-time explanations about cloud upload.
uncertainty_note: Unawareness node id is based on best judgement; retrieved context did not include the U subtree.

title: Uploading home camera clips to cloud storage may exceed necessity or user expectations
description: Home camera footage is highly intrusive personal data. Sending clips to cloud storage may be unnecessary for the stated purpose if local-only storage, minimization, redaction, or shorter retention would suffice. This can create a risk that processing is disproportionate to the purpose and not compliant with data minimization or storage limitation expectations.
assumptions: The system could provide less intrusive alternatives or minimization measures but uploads full clips by default.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance node id is selected by best judgement due to missing retrieved subtree details.

title: Unnecessary disclosure of detailed motion-event data to backend
description: The Home Hub forwards a real-time motion alert to the mobile app backend. If the alert includes more personal data than strictly needed for notification handling (e.g., precise timestamps, room/device identifiers, continuous event metadata, occupancy inferences, or household context), the transfer constitutes an avoidable disclosure of personal data across the P1→P2 boundary.
assumptions: Assumes the motion alert relates to activity in a private home and therefore contains or implies personal data about occupants' presence or behavior.

title: Implicit disclosure of occupancy and behavior patterns via motion-alert metadata
description: Even if the payload is limited to a simple motion alert, the timing, frequency, device/source identifier, and recurrence of alerts sent from the Home Hub to the backend can reveal sensitive patterns such as when residents are home, asleep, away, or moving between areas. This is an implicit and potentially avoidable disclosure caused by metadata and derived inferences from the transfer.
assumptions: Assumes the backend can observe and retain alert timing and source metadata over time.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selection is based on best judgment for implicit/derived disclosure because the retrieved context did not include the full Dd subtree.

title: Notification content may disclose personal activity on the lock screen or to bystanders
description: A motion-detected push notification can reveal that someone is at or near the home, and implicitly that the homeowner is away or monitoring the property. If the notification text is shown on the phone lock screen, wearable, or other synced device, personal household activity is disclosed beyond what is strictly necessary for alerting.
assumptions: Assumes notification content includes event details such as 'motion detected' and may be displayed outside the app before authentication.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-judgement based on LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure decomposition; exact subnode naming may vary by edition.

title: Repeated motion notifications enable inference of occupancy patterns
description: Even if each notification contains minimal text, the timing and frequency of motion alerts sent to the homeowner can allow inference about daily routines, home occupancy, sleep schedules, travel, or the presence of visitors. This creates privacy risk through metadata and event-pattern analysis on this flow.
assumptions: Assumes motion events occur over time and notification timestamps are visible to the recipient device or service providers involved in push delivery.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is a best-judgement selection for inference from event metadata; confidence in the threat is higher than confidence in the precise subnode id.

title: Insufficient transparency about push delivery and lock-screen exposure
description: The homeowner may not understand that motion notifications are delivered via platform push services and can appear on lock screens, secondary devices, or notification histories. If the system does not clearly inform the user about these disclosure paths and visibility settings, processing on this flow is insufficiently transparent.
assumptions: Assumes the app uses standard mobile push infrastructure and does not fully explain notification visibility and routing.
uncertainty_note: Transparency is plausible for this flow, but applicability depends on the product's notice and settings UX; tree-node id is approximate.

title: Pushing detailed motion events without necessity or granular consent may exceed user expectations
description: If the backend sends detailed motion notifications by default, without a clear choice over whether to receive them, how much detail they include, or when they are muted, the flow may process and disclose more personal data than necessary and without sufficiently specific consent or user control.
assumptions: Assumes notifications are enabled by default or detail level cannot be configured by the homeowner.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends strongly on jurisdiction and actual consent/settings design; tree-node id is best-judgement.

title: Shared analytics may remain linkable to app instances or users
description: Although described as aggregated device-usage analytics, the backend's disclosure to the analytics vendor may still include persistent identifiers, stable device attributes, small-cohort dimensions, or repeated contribution patterns that allow records to be linked back to the same device, account, or household over time.
assumptions: Assumes the exported analytics are not fully anonymized and may contain stable pseudonymous identifiers, timestamps, or high-dimensional event attributes.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-judgement based on standard LINDDUN linkability decomposition; exact node naming may differ in the reference tree.

title: Aggregated analytics may still identify individuals or devices
description: If aggregation thresholds are weak or dimensions are too granular, the shared analytics can enable singling out or inference of a specific user/device, especially in low-volume segments or when combined with the vendor's existing datasets.
assumptions: Assumes group sizes may be small or analytics dimensions may include rare combinations such as region, device model, app version, and time window.
uncertainty_note: Applies only if aggregation is insufficient to prevent singling out; exact threat-tree node id may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Disclosure of usage behavior to a third-party vendor
description: Sending device-usage analytics to an external analytics provider exposes user behavior patterns to a separate organization. Even when aggregated, the dataset may reveal product usage trends, feature adoption, geography, or sensitive behavioral insights beyond what users expect to be shared externally.
assumptions: Assumes the vendor is a separate controller/processor and receives access to the analytics content rather than only acting as a blind transport service.
uncertainty_note: High confidence that third-party disclosure risk exists for this flow; exact sub-node id is best-judgement.

title: Users may be unaware that analytics are shared with an external vendor
description: The destination's receipt of analytics by a cloud analytics vendor may be non-transparent to users if notices describe analytics only generically or do not clearly name external recipients, purposes, retention, and combination practices. This limits users' ability to understand the processing.
assumptions: Assumes privacy notices or in-app disclosures do not clearly explain this vendor sharing arrangement.
uncertainty_note: Located at the destination because the risk materializes in the vendor's opaque downstream processing; exact tree-node id may differ.

title: Vendor processing may be incompatible with stated purpose or legal basis
description: Once the analytics vendor receives the data, it may process, retain, enrich, or reuse the analytics for broader benchmarking, service improvement, profiling, or cross-client analysis in ways that exceed the original app purpose or the user's consent/expected legal basis.
assumptions: Assumes contractual, purpose-limitation, retention, and processor-use restrictions are absent, weak, or not technically enforced.
uncertainty_note: This is a common compliance risk for third-party analytics sharing, but whether it applies here depends on actual contracts, configuration, and notices.

title: Backend can infer intimate household patterns from retrieved video clips
description: When P2 retrieves stored video clips for playback, it gains access to highly revealing content and metadata (e.g., timestamps, camera location, motion events). This enables inference about occupants’ presence, routines, visitors, and behaviors beyond what is strictly needed to stream the clip, especially if retrieval events or metadata are retained or further analyzed.
assumptions: Assumes the backend has access to clip content and/or associated metadata rather than acting as a blind pass-through.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selected by best judgment; exact LINDDUN Pro node id may vary depending on the threat-tree version.

title: Video retrieval exposes highly identifying visual and contextual data
description: The backend’s receipt of a stored video clip may disclose directly or indirectly identifying information about residents or visitors, such as faces, voices, home interior details, address clues, daily schedules, and device identifiers embedded in metadata. If the backend processes or logs this data unnecessarily, individuals may become identifiable to parties operating or accessing P2.
assumptions: Assumes video clips or metadata contain personal data and that P2 can access them in intelligible form.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is based on best-fit judgment for disclosure of personal data at the receiving process.

title: Backend-side retrieval logs enable detection of homeowner activity
description: Each retrieval from cloud storage to P2 can reveal that a homeowner is currently viewing security footage, and repeated retrievals can expose patterns such as periods of concern, occupancy checks, or response to incidents. Even if clip content is protected, access timing, frequency, and camera-selection metadata can allow detection of sensitive behavior.
assumptions: Assumes P2 or adjacent infrastructure logs clip retrieval events, timestamps, account identifiers, or camera identifiers.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id may differ across LINDDUN Pro versions; threat applicability depends on whether retrieval metadata is logged.

title: Clip retrieval may be used for secondary purposes incompatible with playback
description: The stated purpose of this flow is to retrieve a stored clip so the homeowner can play it back. A privacy threat arises if P2 reuses the retrieved video or metadata for analytics, model training, employee review, law-enforcement sharing, product improvement, or profiling without a compatible purpose basis or adequate user expectation management.
assumptions: Assumes the service may retain or repurpose retrieved clips/metadata beyond transient delivery for playback.
uncertainty_note: Purpose-limitation node id chosen by best judgment; exact numbering may differ.

title: Playback retrieval may exceed consented or expected processing scope
description: Users may expect stored clips to be fetched only to fulfill an explicit playback request. If P2 retrieves additional clips, associated metadata, or content for background processing, recommendation features, diagnostics, or other non-essential purposes without valid consent or another lawful basis, the flow can violate consent and choice requirements.
assumptions: Assumes consent or user expectation is limited to on-demand playback and that additional backend processing is possible.
uncertainty_note: Node id is an approximate best fit for non-compliance/consent issues in this interaction.
